title: Of vain subtleties
paragraphs: There is a class of little tricks and frivolous subtleties from which men sometimes hope to earn reputation and applause — like the poets who compose whole poems with every line beginning with the same letter. We see the shapes of eggs, globes, wings, and hatchets cut out by the ancient Greeks by the measure of their verses, lengthened or shortened to make this or that figure. Of this kind was the labour of the man whose business it was to count up how many different orders the letters of the alphabet could be transposed in, and who arrived at the incredible total Plutarch reports. I am very taken with the spirit of the man,

["Alexander, as may be seen in Quintilian, Institut. Orat., bk. ii., ch. 20, where he defines Maratarexvia as a certain unnecessary imitation of art, which really does neither good nor harm but is as pointless and ridiculous as the labour of the man who had so perfectly learned to throw small peas through the eye of a needle at a good distance that he never missed one, and was justly rewarded for it, as the story goes, by Alexander, who watched the performance, with a bushel of peas." — Coste.]

who, when a man was brought before him who had learned to throw a grain of millet with such dexterity and surety that he never missed the eye of a needle, and who was afterwards begged to give something as a reward for so rare a feat, ordered — pleasantly, and in my view quite justly — a certain number of bushels of the same grain to be delivered to him, so he would not lack what to practise so famous an art on. It is a strong sign of weak judgement when men admire things just because they are rare and new, or because they are difficult, without any merit or usefulness joined to recommend them.

I have just come from playing with my own family at a game of finding the most things that touch at both extremities. "Sire," for instance, is a title given to the greatest man in the nation, the king, and also to the lowliest, like merchants — but never to anyone of any rank in between. Women of high birth are called Dames, lesser gentlewomen Demoiselles, and the meanest sort of women Dames again, like the first. The cloth of state above our tables is allowed only in the palaces of princes and in taverns. Democritus said that gods and beasts have sharper senses than men, who are in the middle. The Romans wore the same clothes at funerals and at feasts. It is quite certain that extreme fear and an extreme rush of courage both equally trouble and loosen the bowels. The nickname "the Trembling" by which they called Sancho XII, king of Navarre, tells us that valour will set the limbs trembling just as fear does. Those who were arming that king — or whoever else, on a like occasion, was apt to fall into the same agitation — tried to settle him down by playing down the danger he was about to face. "You don't understand me," he said, "for if my flesh could know the danger my courage will straight away carry it into, it would sink to the ground." The faintness that overtakes us in the exercises of Venus, from coldness or distaste, also comes from too violent a desire and an immoderate heat. Extreme cold and extreme heat both scald and roast. Aristotle says that lead pigs will melt and run with cold and the harshness of winter just as with a strong heat. Desire and satiety fill all the gradations above and below pleasure with pain. Stupidity and wisdom meet at the same midpoint of feeling and resolution in the bearing of life's accidents: the wise master and triumph over ill, the others never know it; the latter, you might say, sit on this side of the accidents, the former go beyond them, having weighed and considered their character, measured and judged them for what they are, and then, by force of a vigorous soul, leapt out of their reach; they look down on them and trample them underfoot, having a solid and well-fortified soul against which the darts of fortune, when they come to strike, must necessarily rebound and blunt themselves, meeting a body in which they can make no impression. The ordinary middling sort of men are lodged between these two extremes, made up of those who notice their evils, feel them, and are not able to bear them. Infancy and decrepitude meet in the weakness of the brain; avarice and prodigality meet in the same thirst and desire to get.

One could say, with some show of truth, that there is a beginner's ignorance that comes before knowledge, and a doctoral ignorance that comes after it — an ignorance that knowledge creates and brings forth at the same moment that it dispatches and destroys the first. Out of average understandings, little curious and little instructed, are made good Christians, who by reverence and obedience simply believe and stay constant in their belief. In the middling understandings and the average sort of capacities, the error of opinion is bred; they follow the look of the first impression and have some colour of reason on their side to charge us with simplicity and stupidity for walking on in the old beaten path — meaning those of us who have not informed ourselves by study. The higher and nobler souls, more solid and more clear-sighted, make up another sort of true believers, who by a long and religious investigation of truth have gained a clearer and more penetrating light into the Scriptures, and have uncovered the mysterious and divine secret of our ecclesiastical polity; and yet we see some who, going by the middle step, have reached that highest degree with marvellous results and confirmation, arriving at the outer limit of Christian intelligence and enjoying their victory with great spiritual consolation, humble acknowledgement of divine favour, reform of manners, and singular modesty. With these I do not mean to rank the others who, to clear themselves of any suspicion of their former errors and to satisfy us that they are sound and firm, become extremely indiscreet and unjust in the pressing of our cause, and disgrace it with endless reproaches of violence and oppression. The plain peasants are good people, and so are the philosophers, or whatever the present age calls them — men of strong and clear reason, whose souls are enriched with a full instruction in profitable sciences. The mongrels, who have despised the first form of the ignorance of letters and have not been able to reach the other (sitting between two stools, as I and many more of us do), are dangerous, foolish, and a nuisance; these are the ones who trouble the world. And that is why I, for my part, retreat as far as I can back towards the first and natural station, which I so vainly tried to advance from.
["The term poesie populaire was used, for the first time, in the French language on this occasion. Montaigne coined the expression and indicated its nature." — Ampere.]

has in it certain artless graces by which she may stand comparison with the greatest beauty of poetry brought to perfection by art — as we see in our Gascon villanelles and in the songs that come to us from peoples who know nothing of any science, not even the use of writing. The middling sort of poetry, between these two, is despised, with no value, honour, or esteem.

But seeing that once a path is opened to the fancy, I have found — as commonly happens — that what we had taken for a difficult exercise and a rare subject turns out to be nothing of the kind, and once the invention warms up it finds out an endless number of parallel examples. I shall only add this: that if these Essays of mine were worth a serious critical judgement, it might then, I think, turn out that they would not much take with common and vulgar minds, nor be very welcome to the singular and excellent sort of men; the first would not understand them enough, and the last too much; so they may hover in the middle region.
